narrationScript: Welcome to Structs, Custom Types, and Arrays of Structs. In programming, especially as your applications become more complex, you'll frequently encounter situations where you need to manage related pieces of information. For instance, imagine building a system to keep track of student records. Each student has a name, an ID number, and a GPA. While you could technically store these in three separate arrays—one for names, one for IDs, and one for GPAs—this approach quickly becomes unwieldy. It's hard to keep track of which name belongs to which ID, and passing all this data around in functions would require multiple arguments. This is precisely where C's `struct`s come to our rescue. A `struct`, short for structure, is a powerful user-defined data type that allows you to bundle different types of data items—like our student's name, ID, and GPA—under a single, cohesive name. Think of it as a custom blueprint for creating variables that can hold a collection of diverse information. In this chapter, we'll explore how to define and declare these custom data types, access their individual components, use `typedef` to make your code even cleaner, and manage entire collections of these custom types using arrays of structs. We'll also dive into the crucial concept of pointers to structs, and finally, we'll see how structs, particularly self-referential ones, form the foundation of dynamic data structures like linked lists.
